name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WORK_ENERGY_AND_POWER_MCQ_Q01 - Work done from force displacement graph

questiontext.text:
A force \(F\) acts on a body of mass \(2\text{ kg}\) moving along the \(x\)-axis. The variation of the force with position \(x\) is shown in the graph below:

What is the total work done by the force in displacing the body from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 10\text{ m}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The force-displacement graph shows:
• For \(x = 0\) to \(x = 4\text{ m}\): constant force \(F = 20\text{ N}\).
• For \(x = 4\text{ m}\) to \(x = 8\text{ m}\): linearly decreasing force from \(F = 20\text{ N}\) to \(F = 0\text{ N}\).
• For \(x = 8\text{ m}\) to \(x = 10\text{ m}\): constant negative force \(F = -10\text{ N}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is along the \(x\)-axis. Work done by a variable force in one dimension is defined as the area under the force-displacement curve. Areas above the displacement axis represent positive work, while areas below the displacement axis represent negative work.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The work done by a spatially varying force is: \[ W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \text{Area under the } F\text{-}x \text{ curve} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Divide the area into three geometric parts:
1. Rectangular region from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 4\text{ m}\): \[ W_1 = \text{height} \times \text{base} = 20\text{ N} \times (4 - 0)\text{ m} = 80\text{ J} \] 2. Triangular region from \(x = 4\text{ m}\) to \(x = 8\text{ m}\): \[ W_2 = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times (8 - 4)\text{ m} \times 20\text{ N} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 20 = 40\text{ J} \] 3. Rectangular region below the axis from \(x = 8\text{ m}\) to \(x = 10\text{ m}\): \[ W_3 = (-10\text{ N}) \times (10 - 8)\text{ m} = -10 \times 2 = -20\text{ J} \] Total work done: \[ W = W_1 + W_2 + W_3 = 80\text{ J} + 40\text{ J} + (-20\text{ J}) = 100\text{ J} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are joules (\(\text{N}\cdot\text{m} = \text{J}\)). The positive work exceeds the opposing work, yielding a net positive work of \(100\text{ J}\).
Final Answer: \(100\text{ J}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WORK_ENERGY_AND_POWER_MCQ_Q02 - Energy of a block spring system

questiontext.text:
A block of mass \(m = 1\text{ kg}\) oscillates horizontally on a frictionless surface while attached to an ideal spring of force constant \(k\). The graph shows the variation of potential energy \(V(x)\) and kinetic energy \(K(x)\) as functions of displacement \(x\):

If the total mechanical energy of the system is \(E = 16\text{ J}\) and the amplitude of oscillation is \(x_m = 0.4\text{ m}\), what is the speed of the block at displacement \(x = 0.2\text{ m}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
• Mass of the block: \(m = 1\text{ kg}\).
• Total mechanical energy: \(E = 16\text{ J}\).
• Maximum displacement (amplitude): \(x_m = 0.4\text{ m}\).
• Position of interest: \(x = 0.2\text{ m} = \frac{x_m}{2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The surface is horizontal and frictionless; the spring is massless and obeys Hooke's law. Mechanical energy \(E = K + V\) is conserved at all points of the motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
• Potential energy of a stretched/compressed spring: \[ V(x) = \frac{1}{2} k x^2 \] • Total mechanical energy (equal to potential energy at maximum displacement): \[ E = \frac{1}{2} k x_m^2 \] • Kinetic energy: \[ K(x) = E - V(x) = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
At \(x = 0.2\text{ m}\), the displacement is exactly half of the maximum amplitude: \[ x = \frac{x_m}{2} \] The potential energy at this position is: \[ V\left(\frac{x_m}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2} k \left(\frac{x_m}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4} \left(\frac{1}{2} k x_m^2\right) = \frac{E}{4} \] Substitute \(E = 16\text{ J}\): \[ V = \frac{16\text{ J}}{4} = 4\text{ J} \] From conservation of total mechanical energy: \[ K = E - V = 16\text{ J} - 4\text{ J} = 12\text{ J} \] Express kinetic energy in terms of speed: \[ \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = 12\text{ J} \] Substitute \(m = 1\text{ kg}\): \[ \frac{1}{2} (1) v^2 = 12 \implies v^2 = 24\text{ m}^2\text{s}^{-2} \implies v = \sqrt{24} = 2\sqrt{6}\text{ m s}^{-1} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The maximum speed at \(x = 0\) is \(\sqrt{2E/m} = \sqrt{32} \approx 5.66\text{ m s}^{-1}\). At \(x = 0.2\text{ m}\), \(v = 2\sqrt{6} \approx 4.90\text{ m s}^{-1}\), which correctly lies between \(0\) and \(v_{\max}\).
Final Answer: \(2\sqrt{6}\text{ m s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WORK_ENERGY_AND_POWER_MCQ_Q03 - Tension ratio in vertical circular motion

questiontext.text:
A bob of mass \(m\) is attached to a light, inextensible string of length \(L\) and whirls in a vertical circle as shown in the schematic diagram:

The bob is projected from the lowest point \(A\) with the minimum speed \(v_0 = \sqrt{5gL}\) required to complete the circular path such that the string slackens only upon reaching the topmost point \(C\). What is the ratio of the string tension at the lowest point \(A\) to the string tension when the string is horizontal at point \(B\), that is, \(\frac{T_A}{T_B}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
• Mass of bob: \(m\).
• Length of light inextensible string: \(L\).
• Speed at lowest point \(A\): \(v_0 = \sqrt{5gL}\).
• Tension at highest point \(C\): \(T_C = 0\) (string becomes slack at \(C\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The string is light and taut except at \(C\). The tension force acts inward along the string and does zero work because it is always perpendicular to displacement. Mechanical energy is conserved under the action of the conservative gravitational force.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
• Conservation of mechanical energy between lowest point \(A\) and any height \(h\): \[ \frac{1}{2}mv_A^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgh \] • Centripetal force from Newton's second law along the radial direction: \[ F_{\text{radial}} = \frac{m v^2}{L} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Tension at the lowest point \(A\): At point \(A\), gravity acts downward and tension acts upward toward the center: \[ T_A - mg = \frac{m v_0^2}{L} \] Substitute \(v_0^2 = 5gL\): \[ T_A = mg + \frac{m(5gL)}{L} = mg + 5mg = 6mg \] 2. Speed and tension at point \(B\) (horizontal string, height \(h = L\)): Conserving mechanical energy between \(A\) and \(B\): \[ \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v_B^2 + mgL \] Substitute \(v_0^2 = 5gL\): \[ \frac{1}{2} m (5gL) = \frac{1}{2} m v_B^2 + mgL \implies \frac{5}{2}gL - gL = \frac{1}{2}v_B^2 \implies v_B^2 = 3gL \] At point \(B\), the string is horizontal. Gravity acts vertically downward, contributing nothing to the radial direction. The string tension alone provides the required centripetal acceleration: \[ T_B = \frac{m v_B^2}{L} = \frac{m(3gL)}{L} = 3mg \] 3. Ratio of tensions: \[ \frac{T_A}{T_B} = \frac{6mg}{3mg} = 2 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The tension is largest at the lowest point (\(6mg\)) and decreases monotonically as the bob ascends, dropping to \(3mg\) at the horizontal level and zero at the top. The ratio is dimensionless and equals \(2 : 1\).
Final Answer: \(2 : 1\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WORK_ENERGY_AND_POWER_MCQ_Q04 - Turning points from potential energy function

questiontext.text:
A particle of mass \(m = 0.2\text{ kg}\) moves along the \(x\)-axis in a region where its potential energy is defined by \(V(x) = 2.5 x^2\text{ J}\) (with \(x\) in metres), as shown in the potential curve below:

If the particle has a total mechanical energy \(E = 10\text{ J}\), what are the turning points of its motion and its maximum speed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
• Mass of the particle: \(m = 0.2\text{ kg}\).
• Potential energy function: \(V(x) = 2.5 x^2\text{ J}\).
• Total mechanical energy: \(E = 10\text{ J}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion is one-dimensional along the \(x\)-axis. Mechanical energy \(E = K + V\) is conserved. Kinetic energy cannot be negative, meaning classical motion is restricted to regions where \(E \ge V(x)\). At the turning points, kinetic energy momentarily vanishes (\(K = 0\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
• Turning points condition: \[ K = 0 \implies V(x) = E \] • Maximum kinetic energy occurs where potential energy is minimum: \[ K_{\max} = E - V_{\min} \] • Maximum speed: \[ v_{\max} = \sqrt{\frac{2 K_{\max}}{m}} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Finding the turning points: Set \(V(x) = E\): \[ 2.5 x^2 = 10 \] Solve for \(x\): \[ x^2 = \frac{10}{2.5} = 4 \implies x = \pm 2\text{ m} \] Thus, the turning points are \(x = -2\text{ m}\) and \(x = +2\text{ m}\).
2. Finding maximum speed: The minimum potential energy is at \(x = 0\), where \(V(0) = 0\). The maximum kinetic energy is: \[ K_{\max} = E - 0 = 10\text{ J} \] Relating kinetic energy to speed: \[ \frac{1}{2} m v_{\max}^2 = 10\text{ J} \] Substitute \(m = 0.2\text{ kg}\): \[ \frac{1}{2} (0.2) v_{\max}^2 = 10 \implies 0.1 v_{\max}^2 = 10 \implies v_{\max}^2 = 100 \implies v_{\max} = 10\text{ m s}^{-1} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At \(x = \pm 2\text{ m}\), \(V = 2.5(4) = 10\text{ J} = E\), so \(K = 0\) and the particle halts and reverses direction. At \(x = 0\), the kinetic energy is \(10\text{ J}\), corresponding to \(10\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Final Answer: Turning points at \(x = \pm 2\text{ m}\) and maximum speed of \(10\text{ m s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WORK_ENERGY_AND_POWER_MCQ_Q05 - Two dimensional elastic collision of spheres

questiontext.text:
A sphere of mass \(m\) moving with initial velocity \(v_0\) along the positive \(x\)-axis undergoes an elastic collision with an identical stationary sphere of mass \(m\), as depicted below:

After the collision, the target sphere is scattered at an angle \(\theta_2 = 30^\circ\) below the incident direction. What is the final speed of the incident sphere, \(v_{1f}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
• Incident sphere mass: \(m_1 = m\), initial velocity: \(\mathbf{v}_{1i} = v_0 \hat{\mathbf{i}}\).
• Target sphere mass: \(m_2 = m\), initial velocity: \(\mathbf{v}_{2i} = 0\).
• Scattering angle of the target sphere: \(\theta_2 = 30^\circ\).
• Nature of collision: perfectly elastic.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion occurs entirely in the \(xy\)-plane. No external forces act on the system during the collision, so total linear momentum is conserved in both the \(x\) and \(y\) directions. The collision is elastic, meaning total kinetic energy is conserved before and after the collision.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
• Linear momentum conservation: \[ m \mathbf{v}_{1i} = m \mathbf{v}_{1f} + m \mathbf{v}_{2f} \implies \mathbf{v}_0 = \mathbf{v}_{1f} + \mathbf{v}_{2f} \] • Kinetic energy conservation for elastic collision between equal masses: \[ \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v_{1f}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m v_{2f}^2 \implies v_0^2 = v_{1f}^2 + v_{2f}^2 \] • Dot product expansion of momentum: \[ v_0^2 = |\mathbf{v}_{1f} + \mathbf{v}_{2f}|^2 = v_{1f}^2 + v_{2f}^2 + 2 \mathbf{v}_{1f} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{2f} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Comparing the momentum expansion with kinetic energy conservation: \[ 2 \mathbf{v}_{1f} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{2f} = 0 \implies \mathbf{v}_{1f} \perp \mathbf{v}_{2f} \] Hence, two identical particles colliding elastically with one initially at rest always scatter at right angles: \[ \theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90^\circ \] Given \(\theta_2 = 30^\circ\), the deflection angle of the incident sphere is: \[ \theta_1 = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ \] Now consider linear momentum conservation perpendicular to the initial line of motion (\(y\)-axis): \[ 0 = m v_{1f} \sin \theta_1 - m v_{2f} \sin \theta_2 \] Divide by \(m\) and substitute the known angles: \[ v_{1f} \sin 60^\circ = v_{2f} \sin 30^\circ \implies v_{1f} \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = v_{2f} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \implies v_{2f} = \sqrt{3} v_{1f} \] Substitute this into the kinetic energy equation: \[ v_{1f}^2 + v_{2f}^2 = v_0^2 \] \[ v_{1f}^2 + (\sqrt{3} v_{1f})^2 = v_0^2 \implies v_{1f}^2 + 3 v_{1f}^2 = v_0^2 \implies 4 v_{1f}^2 = v_0^2 \] Taking the positive square root: \[ v_{1f} = \frac{v_0}{2} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The target ball speed is \(v_{2f} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} v_0\). Momentum along \(x\) is \(v_{1f}\cos 60^\circ + v_{2f}\cos 30^\circ = \frac{v_0}{4} + \frac{3v_0}{4} = v_0\), exactly matching the initial momentum. Total kinetic energy is also preserved: \(\left(\frac{v_0}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}v_0}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{v_0^2}{4} + \frac{3v_0^2}{4} = v_0^2\).
Final Answer: \(\frac{v_0}{2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_WORK_ENERGY_AND_POWER_MCQ_Q06 - Maximum compression of spring with friction

questiontext.text:
A block of mass \(m = 2\text{ kg}\) moves along a rough horizontal surface with speed \(v = 4\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and collides with a horizontally mounted ideal spring of spring constant \(k = 40\text{ N m}^{-1}\), as shown in the figure:

The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is \(\mu = 0.2\). Taking acceleration due to gravity \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the maximum compression of the spring?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
• Mass of block: \(m = 2\text{ kg}\).
• Initial speed: \(v = 4\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
• Spring constant: \(k = 40\text{ N m}^{-1}\).
• Coefficient of kinetic friction: \(\mu = 0.2\).
• Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\).
• Final speed at maximum compression \(x_m\): \(v_f = 0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The motion is horizontal. During compression, both the restoring force of the spring and the kinetic friction force act in the direction opposing the compression of the spring. We apply the work-energy theorem, which accounts for work done by both conservative and non-conservative forces.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
• Work-energy theorem: \[ W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i = 0 - \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \] • Work done by the spring force over compression \(x_m\): \[ W_s = -\frac{1}{2} k x_m^2 \] • Work done by the kinetic friction force: \[ W_f = -f_k x_m = -\mu m g x_m \] • Net work done: \[ W_{\text{net}} = W_s + W_f = -\frac{1}{2} k x_m^2 - \mu m g x_m \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Equate the net work done to the change in kinetic energy: \[ -\frac{1}{2} k x_m^2 - \mu m g x_m = -\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \] Multiply the entire equation by \(-2\): \[ k x_m^2 + 2 \mu m g x_m - m v^2 = 0 \] Calculate the numerical coefficients:
• \(k = 40\text{ N m}^{-1}\)
• \(2 \mu m g = 2 \times 0.2 \times 2\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m s}^{-2} = 8\text{ N}\)
• \(m v^2 = 2\text{ kg} \times (4\text{ m s}^{-1})^2 = 32\text{ J}\) Substitute these into the quadratic equation: \[ 40 x_m^2 + 8 x_m - 32 = 0 \] Divide through by \(8\): \[ 5 x_m^2 + x_m - 4 = 0 \] Factor the quadratic equation: \[ (5 x_m - 4)(x_m + 1) = 0 \] Since the physical compression must be positive (\(x_m > 0\)): \[ 5 x_m - 4 = 0 \implies x_m = \frac{4}{5}\text{ m} = 0.8\text{ m} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verify the energy balance at \(x_m = 0.8\text{ m}\):
• Potential energy stored in the spring: \(\frac{1}{2} k x_m^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times (0.8)^2 = 20 \times 0.64 = 12.8\text{ J}\).
• Energy dissipated by friction: \(\mu m g x_m = 0.2 \times 2 \times 10 \times 0.8 = 3.2\text{ J}\).
• Total energy accounted for: \(12.8\text{ J} + 3.2\text{ J} = 16.0\text{ J}\).
• Initial kinetic energy: \(\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 4^2 = 16.0\text{ J}\). The energy accounting is exact.
Final Answer: \(0.8\text{ m}\)
